why:
Use this repertoire when Black answers your king pawn with the Sicilian c-pawn. Keep the London and Vienna as separate choices; sharing the first move does not make their later plans interchangeable.

The Grand Prix approach develops the queen-side knight and usually advances the f-pawn. That gains king-side space and controls e5, but also weakens diagonals around your king. The bishop may develop actively or quietly depending on Black's reply. Complete development and meet central threats before attacking.

Black often has central counterplay with the d-pawn. Do not play the same pawn sequence automatically: the early knight attack on e4 is one example where a concrete central response comes first. The deeper branches are level-gated, and an attack is never promised.
